screens.title: What is AWS CodeCommit?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CodeCommit is a fully managed source control service that hosts private Git repositories for your team. At its core it behaves like any Git server — you use clone, add, commit, push, and pull — but AWS manages the infrastructure, storage, and scaling for you. This removes the operational burden of running your own Git servers and integrates repository encryption and access control with AWS services. For example, repositories are encrypted at rest with KMS, and network traffic is protected with HTTPS or SSH. Using CodeCommit also means your IAM setup controls who can read or write a repo, and you can combine repository events with other AWS services for automation. A common misconception is that CodeCommit changes Git workflows; it does not. It preserves standard Git semantics, so existing clients and CI systems continue to work. A concrete example: a developer clones a CodeCommit repo with a generated HTTPS username and password, makes a feature change, commits locally, and pushes the branch back to CodeCommit where a pull request triggers automated tests. Takeaway: CodeCommit gives you managed hosting and AWS-native security while keeping familiar Git workflows intact.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › What is CodeCommit?
Managed Git hosting with AWS security
CodeCommit stores repositories, handles replication and scaling, and integrates with KMS and IAM to protect your code.
Key behaviors
  • Supports standard Git protocols and commands, so client workflows remain unchanged.
  • Encrypts repos at rest using KMS and secures transport via HTTPS or SSH.
  • Integrates with IAM for fine-grained access control and with other AWS services for automation.
Analogy
Think of CodeCommit as a private GitHub inside your AWS account. The workflow is the same, but AWS manages storage and security.
Example
# Clone a CodeCommit repository (HTTPS or SSH URL)
git clone https://git-codecommit.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/v1/repos/my-first-ci-cd-app
cd my-first-ci-cd-app
# Make changes, stage, commit, and push
git add README.md
git commit -m "feat: add feature section"
git push origin feature/add-new-content
Key Takeaway

CodeCommit keeps your Git workflow unchanged while giving AWS-managed security and scaling. Use IAM and KMS to control access and protect data.

screens.title: Authentication methods: HTTPS vs SSH
screens.narratorSegment: CodeCommit supports two primary authentication methods for Git operations: HTTPS credentials issued from IAM and SSH keys uploaded to IAM. HTTPS credentials are a username and password pair you generate in the IAM console specifically for CodeCommit. They are easy to set up and convenient for individual developers or new machines. However, they are static credentials—treat them like any password and rotate or revoke them when needed. SSH uses a public/private key pair; you upload the public key to IAM and keep the private key on your machine or automation host. SSH is a preferred option for automated systems like CI servers because it supports key-based authentication without interactive prompts. Both methods are protected by IAM policies that control permissions such as codecommit:GitPull and codecommit:GitPush. A common misconception is that HTTPS is insecure; in fact, HTTPS transmits over TLS and can be safe when credentials are managed properly. Example: for a build server that only needs to check out source, grant an IAM role or user only codecommit:GitPull permissions and use SSH keys or a temporary credential mechanism if available. Takeaway: pick HTTPS for simple personal setups and SSH for automation and stronger key control.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Authentication
HTTPS Credentials
Generated username and password via IAM for Git over HTTPS.
  • Easy to create in the IAM console and use with most Git clients.
  • Good for personal use or occasional pushes from developer machines.
  • Rotate or revoke when compromised; follows standard credential hygiene.
# Example: push via HTTPS (you will enter credentials)
git clone https://git-codecommit.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/v1/repos/my-first-ci-cd-app
# make edits
git add .
git commit -m "docs: update readme"
git push origin main
SSH Keys
Upload your public SSH key to IAM and authenticate using your private key for key-based Git access.
  • Preferred for automation and CI servers due to non-interactive key usage.
  • Keep private keys secure and limit which hosts can use them.
  • Combine with IAM policies to restrict repository actions.
# Example SSH clone
# configure SSH config to use the private key and CodeCommit host
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -f ~/.ssh/codecommit_key
# upload the public key to IAM, then:
git clone ssh://git-codecommit.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/v1/repos/my-first-ci-cd-app
Common mistake

Treat credentials like passwords—rotate and revoke them, and prefer SSH keys or temporary credentials for automated systems to reduce exposure.

screens.title: IAM and permissions for CodeCommit
screens.narratorSegment: IAM is the central control plane for CodeCommit access. Permissions are expressed in IAM policies that you attach to users, groups, or roles. Typical permissions include codecommit:GitPull for read-only access, codecommit:GitPush for write access, and higher-level management permissions for administering repositories. In practice you should follow the principle of least privilege: give developers the minimum set of permissions they need and give CI/CD systems only the permissions required for their job. For example, a CI build agent that only checks out source for tests should receive codecommit:GitPull on the specific repository rather than repository-wide write permissions. A common misconception is that IAM policies are optional; they are required to allow Git operations, because CodeCommit enforces IAM checks. A concrete example: create an IAM policy granting codecommit:GitPull and attach it to the role assumed by your build server. Then verify the build can clone but cannot push. Takeaway: design IAM policies that map to roles—developer, reviewer, build server—and test access to avoid over-permissioned principals. IAM and permissions for CodeCommit means use iam policies to grant specific codecommit actions. apply least privilege and assign roles for developers, reviewers, and automated systems.. In practical terms, granting least-privilege access to users, roles, and ci/cd systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Needs pull and push permissions for active feature development.

May only need read access to review changes and run tests locally.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",

Avoid attaching broad permissions to users or roles. Overly permissive policies risk accidental or malicious changes in repositories.

screens.title: Standard Git workflow with CodeCommit
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a typical Git workflow against a CodeCommit repository and what each step accomplishes. Start by cloning the repository using the CodeCommit HTTPS or SSH URL. Cloning creates a local copy and sets origin to the CodeCommit remote. After editing files, stage them with git add so the index records changes. Then create a commit with git commit -m "message"; that creates a local snapshot with a message and metadata. To share work, push your branch with git push origin feature/branch — this uploads commits to CodeCommit. To retrieve others' work, run git pull origin branch to fetch and merge remote changes. A common mistake is forgetting to configure credentials, causing authentication failures at push or pull time. Another issue is accidentally committing sensitive files; add them to. gitignore before committing. Example: create README changes, add and commit, then push a new branch and open a pull request. Takeaway: every Git command has a clear role—local staging, snapshot, or remote synchronization—and correct credentials and branch discipline make the workflow predictable for teams. Standard Git workflow with CodeCommit means use standard git commands with codecommit. ensure credentials are configured and branches are used to isolate work before merging via pull requests.. In practical terms, clone, add, commit, push, and pull — exact commands and expected outcomes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Branching strategy and feature branches
screens.narratorSegment: Branching keeps work isolated so features and fixes can progress without destabilizing the main branch. A simple and effective strategy is to create short-lived feature branches named feature/description or fix/issue-number. This makes it easy to scan branch lists and understand intent. Start a branch with git checkout -b feature/name, do your work, and push it to CodeCommit for review. Once a pull request is approved and automated checks pass, merge into main using an agreed strategy such as fast-forward or squash merges depending on your team's history preference. A common misconception is that more branches equal better organization; in reality, uncontrolled long-lived branches increase merge conflicts. Favor short-lived branches and frequent merges. Example: developer A creates feature/add-login, pushes commits, opens a pull request, another developer approves, automated tests run, and the branch is merged. Takeaway: consistent naming, short-lived branches, and enforced pull requests keep a healthy repository and reduce integration pain. Branching strategy and feature branches means use short-lived feature branches with descriptive names, protect main with pull requests and automated checks to reduce merge conflicts.. In practical terms, isolate work with branches and follow a predictable naming and merge practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Recommended branch lifecycle

screens.title: Pull requests and approval rules
screens.narratorSegment: Pull requests in CodeCommit are the formal mechanism to propose changes, invite reviewers, and run checks before merging into a target branch. When you open a pull request you select the source and destination branches, provide a title and description, and optionally assign reviewers. Approval rules can be attached to repositories or branches to require a minimum number of approvals or specific approvers before a merge is allowed. This helps enforce code quality and compliance standards. Automated checks, such as CI pipelines, should be wired to run on pull requests so tests and linters validate the change before approval. A common misconception is that pull requests are optional overhead; in collaborative environments they are a critical quality gate. Example: set an approval rule that requires two approvals from senior developers for changes to main. If a developer attempts to merge without sufficient approvals, CodeCommit rejects the merge. Takeaway: use pull requests and approval rules to protect critical branches and integrate automated testing for reliable merges. Pull requests and approval rules means pull requests plus approval rules ensure code review and automated checks run before merges to protected branches, reducing risky changes.. screens.title: Encryption and transport security
screens.narratorSegment: Security is multi-layered in CodeCommit. Repositories are encrypted at rest using AWS KMS keys, which ensures stored objects cannot be read by someone without the appropriate KMS permissions. In transit, Git traffic is protected by TLS when using HTTPS and by the SSH protocol when using SSH-based authentication. Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Encryption & Transport
Encryption at rest
CodeCommit uses KMS to encrypt repository data on disk. Access to decrypt these objects is governed by KMS policies and IAM permissions.
  • Protects stored objects from unauthorized reading even if storage is accessed directly.
  • Use separate KMS keys for audit and separation of duties when required.
Transport security
HTTPS uses TLS to secure traffic; SSH uses key-based encryption for the transport layer. Both prevent eavesdropping during pushes and pulls.
Practical advice
Do not conflate encryption with access control: keep IAM policies strict and rotate credentials or revoke SSH keys when a machine is decommissioned.
Check

If a user cannot access a repo, verify both IAM permissions and that their transport credentials (HTTPS or SSH) are configured correctly.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting CodeCommit often centers on authentication, branch mistakes, and merge conflicts. If you see an "Authentication failed" error while using HTTPS, the most likely cause is that HTTPS Git credentials were not generated and configured in IAM. For SSH-related failures, confirm the public key is uploaded and the private key is accessible by your Git client. Another frequent issue is pushing directly to main without a pull request; this can bypass reviews and introduce defects. Protect main with approval rules to avoid accidental direct pushes. Merge conflicts happen when two developers edit the same lines; resolve them locally, test the combined changes, commit a merge, and push the resolved branch. A misconception is that CodeCommit causes conflicts; conflicts arise from concurrent edits and are inherent to Git. Example troubleshooting steps: verify remote URL with git remote -v, test authentication with a simple git ls-remote, and check IAM policies for missing codecommit:Git* permissions. Takeaway: identify whether the problem is credential, permission, or workflow-related, then apply the small corrective actions outlined above. Common mistakes and troubleshooting means check credentials, confirm iam permissions, protect main branch, and resolve conflicts locally before pushing merged changes.. screens.title: Integrating CodeCommit with CI/CD
screens.narratorSegment: CodeCommit integrates naturally with pipelines: a pushed branch or opened pull request can trigger a CI pipeline to run tests and linters. In this setup, the pipeline assumes an IAM role with minimal permissions necessary to access the repository, such as codecommit:GitPull. Avoid giving the pipeline unnecessary write permissions unless it needs to push artifacts or tags. For build servers that must run tests on every pull request, configure the pipeline to fetch the source from CodeCommit and report status back to the pull request so reviewers can see test results. A common error is attaching user credentials to the pipeline instead of a role; prefer IAM roles that grant temporary credentials and are easier to revoke or rotate. Takeaway: design the pipeline's IAM role narrowly, use PR-triggered builds to gate merges, and report results into pull requests to close the feedback loop. fullNarratorScript:
Today you'll learn how AWS CodeCommit gives you a secure, scalable place to host private Git repositories while letting you keep familiar Git workflows. We'll cover authentication methods, how IAM gates access, the standard clone-add-commit-push lifecycle, and how branches and pull requests support collaboration. You'll see concrete examples: generating HTTPS credentials in IAM, uploading SSH public keys, staging and committing a change, and creating a pull request for review. We'll also discuss common mistakes like missing credentials or pushing directly to protected branches, and practical safeguards such as approval rules and least-privilege IAM policies. This chapter matters because source control is where teams coordinate changes, run automated tests, and protect production branches. By the end you'll be able to connect your local Git client to CodeCommit, choose the right authentication method for your workflow, and follow branching practices that reduce conflicts and improve code quality. Think about the last time a merge caused a problem; the practices here reduce that risk and make collaboration predictable.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use immediately. First, you will be able to create and manage Git repositories inside CodeCommit. That means setting up a repository in the AWS console, cloning it locally, and understanding repository settings. Second, you will implement secure authentication to CodeCommit using IAM controls: generate HTTPS Git credentials, upload SSH public keys, and assign the appropriate IAM policies. Third, you will confidently apply core Git commands—clone, add, commit, push, and pull—to move code between your machine and CodeCommit. We'll show exact command examples and common errors to avoid. Fourth, you will manage branches and pull requests, including creating feature branches, opening pull requests, and configuring approval rules to enforce code review. Each objective links a concrete action to its practical reason: better security, predictable collaboration, and lower production risk. As you work through the exercises, verify competency by completing the Branching, Committing, and Pull Request activity so you can prove each skill end-to-end.

This second objectives slide links each learning goal to a concrete practice and common pitfall. When you create and manage a repository, test it by cloning and verifying remote branches exist; otherwise you may push to the wrong remote. For secure access, practice both HTTPS credentials and SSH keys — HTTPS is quick for personal use, SSH is stronger for automation; a common mistake is leaving unused credentials active. For Git commands, run the clone-add-commit-push cycle and learn how to recover from credential errors or merge conflicts. For branching and pull requests, create a feature branch, open a pull request, and try approval rules so you see enforcement in action. Each task closes the feedback loop: you perform an action, observe CodeCommit behavior, and fix issues like missing IAM permissions or misconfigured remotes. These practices reduce accidental direct pushes to main and help your team maintain code quality.

AWS CodeCommit is a fully managed source control service that hosts private Git repositories for your team. At its core it behaves like any Git server — you use clone, add, commit, push, and pull — but AWS manages the infrastructure, storage, and scaling for you. This removes the operational burden of running your own Git servers and integrates repository encryption and access control with AWS services. For example, repositories are encrypted at rest with KMS, and network traffic is protected with HTTPS or SSH. Using CodeCommit also means your IAM setup controls who can read or write a repo, and you can combine repository events with other AWS services for automation. A common misconception is that CodeCommit changes Git workflows; it does not. It preserves standard Git semantics, so existing clients and CI systems continue to work. A concrete example: a developer clones a CodeCommit repo with a generated HTTPS username and password, makes a feature change, commits locally, and pushes the branch back to CodeCommit where a pull request triggers automated tests. Takeaway: CodeCommit gives you managed hosting and AWS-native security while keeping familiar Git workflows intact.

CodeCommit supports two primary authentication methods for Git operations: HTTPS credentials issued from IAM and SSH keys uploaded to IAM. HTTPS credentials are a username and password pair you generate in the IAM console specifically for CodeCommit. They are easy to set up and convenient for individual developers or new machines. However, they are static credentials—treat them like any password and rotate or revoke them when needed. SSH uses a public/private key pair; you upload the public key to IAM and keep the private key on your machine or automation host. SSH is a preferred option for automated systems like CI servers because it supports key-based authentication without interactive prompts. Both methods are protected by IAM policies that control permissions such as codecommit:GitPull and codecommit:GitPush. A common misconception is that HTTPS is insecure; in fact, HTTPS transmits over TLS and can be safe when credentials are managed properly. Example: for a build server that only needs to check out source, grant an IAM role or user only codecommit:GitPull permissions and use SSH keys or a temporary credential mechanism if available. Takeaway: pick HTTPS for simple personal setups and SSH for automation and stronger key control.

IAM is the central control plane for CodeCommit access. Permissions are expressed in IAM policies that you attach to users, groups, or roles. Typical permissions include codecommit:GitPull for read-only access, codecommit:GitPush for write access, and higher-level management permissions for administering repositories. In practice you should follow the principle of least privilege: give developers the minimum set of permissions they need and give CI/CD systems only the permissions required for their job. For example, a CI build agent that only checks out source for tests should receive codecommit:GitPull on the specific repository rather than repository-wide write permissions. A common misconception is that IAM policies are optional; they are required to allow Git operations, because CodeCommit enforces IAM checks. A concrete example: create an IAM policy granting codecommit:GitPull and attach it to the role assumed by your build server. Then verify the build can clone but cannot push. Takeaway: design IAM policies that map to roles—developer, reviewer, build server—and test access to avoid over-permissioned principals. In practical terms, granting least-privilege access to users, roles, and ci/cd systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cloning creates a local copy and sets origin to the CodeCommit remote. After editing files, stage them with git add so the index records changes. Then create a commit with git commit -m "message"; that creates a local snapshot with a message and metadata. To share work, push your branch with git push origin feature/branch — this uploads commits to CodeCommit. To retrieve others' work, run git pull origin branch to fetch and merge remote changes. A simple and effective strategy is to create short-lived feature branches named feature/description or fix/issue-number. This makes it easy to scan branch lists and understand intent. Start a branch with git checkout -b feature/name, do your work, and push it to CodeCommit for review.
